title: Truth teaches (Imitation 1.3)
hookLine: happy is the one whom truth teaches directly
tomorrow: where's a kingdom you can't point to on a map?

cards: A screenshot goes around the group chat, and three friends offer three readings of one short reply. Everyone's an interpreter; nobody asks the person who sent it.

The third chapter of the Imitation has a strange detail for that moment. It's a book, made entirely of words, and it says the best teacher isn't words at all. Happy, it says, is the one whom truth teaches directly.
So who's doing the teaching, once the books run out?

teach.b: The chapter's opening, in its sense: happy is the one whom truth teaches by itself, not through figures and words that pass away, but as it really is.
Our own opinions and senses, it says, often fool us, and see very little. Then the puzzle's answer: the teacher is a someone.
The one to whom the eternal Word speaks is set free from a crowd of opinions. From that one Word all things come, and all things speak of him.
That's the language of John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
So a book can say this without tripping over itself. It's pointing past its own pages, like a friend who says: don't take my word for it, go and meet him. And it's careful not to sneer at study.
Learning isn't to be blamed, it says; knowledge is good in itself.
But a good conscience and a good life come first, and a humble knowledge of yourself is a surer road to God than deep searching after learning.
Then a glance at the well-known teachers of its day: where are they now? Others hold their places and hardly think of them.

how: Some Christians pair reading with silent prayer, so that what they read can be listened to and not only studied; the Imitation is often read that way, a chapter at a time.

o: picking the right expert and trusting them
truth itself teaching you directly, as it is
a rule that teachers must always be honest

p: often fool us and see very little
good in itself, but not first

s: for the Imitation, truth is mainly a set of correct statements
that's the likely assumption. here the teacher is the eternal Word: someone who speaks.
the Imitation says learning is to be blamed
it says learning isn't to be blamed; a good conscience and a good life just come first.
the chapter echoes the opening of John's Gospel
in the beginning was the Word: from that one Word, it says, all things come.

games.q: two friends have argued for an hour over what one Bible verse really means, trading commentaries. by the Imitation's third chapter, what's the better next step?
o: find a third commentary to break the tie.
stop arguing and sit quietly with the verse itself.
agree the verse can't really mean anything.
games.why: opinions see very little, the chapter says; the one to whom the eternal Word speaks is set free from a crowd of them.

practice: Set the words down for the sit. Choose one sound around you, a fan, traffic, a bird, your own breath, and let it be exactly what it is, without naming or explaining it. If you pray, you can simply listen.

wordCard.voice: Truth teaches. The Imitation's hope that truth itself, the eternal Word, teaches a person directly, as it is.
